source.title: AstroPT: Scaling Large Observation Models for Astronomy
source.authors: Michael J. Smith; Ryan J Roberts; Eirini Angeloudi; M. Huertas-Company

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in an astronomical image-modeling setting, extending the question beyond text pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study's own results are validation-loss curves for AstroPT models and linear-probe performance across model sizes. Prior language scaling laws discussed in the text are background, not results from this study. The loss objective is Huber loss, not cross-entropy.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own astronomical-image pretraining loss curves and downstream scaling results, testing V5 and V6 in a new modality. Its explicitly reported loss saturation also bears on V7's curve-bending component.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report saturating log-log pretraining-loss scaling and improved downstream linear-probe performance with compute up to approximately 89M parameters. They conclude that autoregressive image-patch prediction learns scientifically useful representations. Their explanation of saturation through dataset information density, and extension to other modalities, remain hypotheses.
record.recipe_differences: Uses astronomical image patches rather than text and predicts the next patch using Huber loss rather than held-out cross-entropy. The study does not implement the original language-model scaling recipe.
record.problems: The loss values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text. The scaling evidence comes from one astronomical dataset and one model/training setup, and the authors attribute the observed saturation tentatively to information density in that dataset. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported correlations.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; the study trains astronomical image models using Huber loss.
Small-run fits predicting losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Fixed-compute allocation experiments and stable compute-optimal parameter and token exponents.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including video, repeated-data scaling and fine-tuning scaling; quantitative power-law fitting and exponent estimation.
Prediction from pretraining loss, extrapolation beyond tested scales, and downstream performance above 89M parameters. Only linear probes on selected astronomical tasks are evaluated.

Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or datasets; explanations of disagreement between published laws. The proposed dataset-information explanation for saturation is not experimentally tested.

record.verdict_notes: Based only on the supplied text. Figure 2's individual curves cannot be reconstructed numerically. Saturation does not distinguish a broken power law from a power law approaching an irreducible loss floor. Shared rows have version-specific states explained in problem fields because the schema permits only one state per row.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses astronomical images and Huber loss, not language models with held-out cross-entropy loss.
It does not fit laws on small runs and use them to predict the loss of larger runs.
It does not compare parameter-token allocations at a fixed compute budget or estimate compute-optimal scaling.
It does not hold parameter count fixed while varying architecture details to measure their effect on loss.
Tests astronomical image pretraining on one dataset and training setup; does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests linear-probe performance on selected astronomical properties across model sizes and compute; does not test downstream language tasks or predict performance from pretraining loss.
It does not vary fitting methods, parameter counting, data, or training schedules to test fit-dependence or disagreement between fitted laws.

relationships.condition: Astronomical-image autoregressive pretraining below the approximately 89M parameter saturation boundary
relationships.reason: R1–R8 record the loss curves that the authors describe as exhibiting log-log scaling; support is qualitative because no power-law fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Loss curves exhibited reported log-log scaling below the approximately 89M-parameter saturation boundary.

relationships.condition: The approximately 89M saturation boundary and larger AstroPT models on this dataset
relationships.reason: R9–R16 fall at or beyond the explicitly reported saturation boundary, qualifying continued improvement under a single power law.
relationships.display_finding: Models around 89M parameters and larger reached the reported saturation boundary, qualifying continued improvement under a single power law.

relationships.condition: Twelve astronomical linear-probe tasks across 1M–89M models
relationships.reason: R17–R28 report positive compute–performance correlations of 0.851–0.998; R23 and R28 also show abrupt gains at 12M, so evidence establishes an in-range trend rather than a smooth extrapolative law.
relationships.display_finding: Compute–performance correlations ranged from 0.851 to 0.998, with abrupt gains at 12M parameters on two tasks rather than uniformly smooth improvement.

relationships.condition: Curve bending toward saturation in astronomical-image pretraining
relationships.reason: R9–R16 and the accompanying Figure 2 discussion explicitly report saturation near 89M after an initial log-log scaling region; this supports only V7's curve-bending component.
relationships.display_finding: An initial log-log scaling region gives way to saturation near 89M parameters.
